lstm_check.criterion: mean validation-years NSE over 12 basins and 3 leads (higher is better)

transformer_check.criterion: mean validation-years NSE over 12 basins and 3 leads (higher is better)

causality.test: Every trained network, evaluation mode: 3 random sequences of 365 days; the inputs after day t are replaced by new random numbers for t = 0, 1, 179, 182, 363 (counted from 0). largest_change_up_to_day_t is the largest absolute change of any output up to day t (scaled flow units; asserted below 1e-5), smallest_change_after_day_t shows that the later outputs do react, and the Transformer without its mask fails the same test.

formulas.symbols: T = days per training sequence (warmup + block), B = sequences per update, n = inputs per day, h = hidden units, d = d_model, f = feed-forward width, L = layers, 3 = leads. One multiply-add = one weight times one number, added to a sum.
formulas.lstm_forward: B x T x [4 x h x (h + n) + 3 x h]: four gates, each a weight matrix of h x (h + n), on every day; plus the output layer.
formulas.transformer_forward: B x [T x n x d + L x (4 x T x d^2 + 2 x T^2 x d + 2 x T x d x f) + 3 x T x d]: input projection; per layer the four attention projections (query, key, value, output), the day-by-day attention (T^2 x d for the scores and T^2 x d for mixing the values, summed over the heads) and the feed-forward block; plus the output layer. The causal mask hides later days but does not save operations: the full T x T table is still computed.
formulas.training_update: Forward pass only. A training update also runs the backward pass, which costs about twice the forward pass, so one update is roughly 3 x the forward count (a rule of thumb, not measured). Biases, layer normalisation and the activation functions are not counted.
formulas.energy: training seconds x 15 W / 3600 = watt-hours. 15 W is the nominal design power of this laptop's processor - an ASSUMPTION, not a measurement; the screen and the rest of the laptop are not included.
formulas.skill: skill = mean over the three leads of the median NSE over the 12 basins; one point of skill = 0.01 NSE.

cost_of_skill.definition: skill = mean over the three leads of the median NSE over the 12 basins; one point of skill = 0.01 NSE.

answer: Accuracy in the test years (median NSE over 12 basins at 1 / 2 / 3 days ahead, average forecast of 2 seeds): LSTM 0.598 / 0.336 / 0.270, Transformer 0.580 / 0.345 / 0.280. Single seeds: LSTM 0.591 to 0.597 / 0.329 to 0.334 / 0.259 to 0.270, Transformer 0.566 to 0.593 / 0.340 to 0.344 / 0.276 to 0.278.

Which is more accurate (differences are Transformer minus LSTM; skill = mean over the three leads of the median NSE): on the validation years, where such a choice has to be made, -0.056 (LSTM 0.307, Transformer 0.251; the single seeds of the two models do not overlap); the trainer's own validation score (mean NSE over basins and leads) is 0.391, 0.387 for the LSTM seeds and 0.377, 0.375 for the Transformer seeds. In the test years +0.000 (LSTM 0.401, Transformer 0.402; the single seeds of the two models overlap: within seed noise). Seeds of the same model differ by up to 0.030 (validation) and 0.011 (test) in this skill. In the mean NSE over the basins, which one basin moves less than the median, the difference is -0.014 on the validation years and -0.000 in the test years (see the note on basins).

By lead in the test years (Transformer minus LSTM, median NSE): 1 day ahead -0.018 (single seeds overlap; LSTM higher in 8 of 12 basins), 2 days ahead +0.009 (single seeds do not overlap; LSTM higher in 5 of 12 basins), 3 days ahead +0.010 (single seeds do not overlap; LSTM higher in 5 of 12 basins).

High-flow warnings in the test years, pooled over the basins, at 1 / 2 / 3 days ahead - share of high-flow days warned: LSTM 61% / 34% / 21%, Transformer 63% / 36% / 23%; share of warnings that were false: LSTM 32% / 38% / 45%, Transformer 35% / 40% / 44%. Onsets only (river still low when the forecast was issued) - warned: LSTM 18% / 8% / 6%, Transformer 14% / 7% / 6%; false among those warnings: LSTM 58% / 55% / 54%, Transformer 59% / 55% / 49%.

Cost to train one model: the Transformer has 68,291 weights against 21,443 (3.2x), needs about 1.87 billion multiply-adds per update (forward pass) against 244 million (7.7x), took 0.573 s per update against 0.038 s (14.9x), reached its best validation score after 800 updates (549 s) against 800 (57 s), and trained for 677 s against 65 s (10.4x; CPU seconds 2040 against 211). At an assumed 15 W that is about 2.82 Wh against 0.27 Wh per model. The learning-rate checks cost another 391 s (Transformer) and 36 s (LSTM).

Cost of one point of skill (0.01 NSE, test years, mean of single seeds): LSTM 1.6 s of training (6.9 mWh assumed), Transformer 17.0 s of training (70.7 mWh assumed) - 10.3 times as much. The extra 612 s of the Transformer buy no skill that stands clear of the seed noise: +0.3 points, while seeds of the same model differ by up to 1.1 points.

Is the Transformer worth it here? No. On the validation years it is less accurate than the LSTM by 0.056 NSE in the median over the basins (single seeds do not overlap; in the mean over the basins the difference is -0.014); in the test years the difference is +0.000 NSE, within seed noise. So it is at best as accurate as the LSTM, and it needs 10.4 times the training time. This holds for this problem size - 12 basins, 20 training years, sequences of 365 days, small networks on a laptop CPU, with only the learning rate checked for each model; with 2 seeds per model the noise estimate is rough. It is not a general verdict on Transformers.
notes: Both networks are trained by flood.fit on the 12 basins together with past weather + river gauge + the ten basin properties (17 inputs per day), sequences of 365 days (180 read before the first scored forecast, 185 scored), 32 sequences per update, at most 1000 updates, a validation check every 100 updates and stop after 6 checks without improvement. Only the network differs.

Update limit: LSTM seed 0, LSTM seed 1, Transformer seed 0, Transformer seed 1 ran to the limit of 1000 updates without the early stop; all of them had their best validation score before the last check. The limit is the same for both networks and was set by the time available on this laptop.

The sequences are 365 days here, not the 730 days of 04_lstm_all.py, because the attention cost grows with the square of the sequence length. cmp_lstm is therefore not the same model as lstm_wq and its scores may differ from results/lstm_all.json.

Settings: each network had only its learning rate checked, in the same way - LSTM [0.001, 0.002], Transformer [0.0003, 0.001], seed 0, at most 300 updates, chosen by the trainer's own validation-years score (mean NSE over 12 basins and 3 leads). The candidates differ by 0.0212 (LSTM) and 0.0117 (Transformer); the final seeds of the chosen setting differ by 0.0033 and 0.0017 in the same score. Fixed without a search: LSTM hidden 64 and dropout 0.2 (the engine defaults); Transformer d_model 64, 2 layers, 4 heads, feed-forward 128, dropout 0.1. For reference, the main all-basin LSTM of 04_lstm_all.py (730-day sequences) uses hidden 64, learning rate 0.002, dropout 0.2.
Neither network had its size, depth or dropout searched: a longer search could change the picture for either model, more likely for the Transformer, which has more settings.

Fair test: scalers, thresholds and weights use the training years 1980-2000; both learning rates and every stopping point were chosen on the validation years 2000-2005; the test years 2005-2014 were scored once, after all choices. Which model is 'better' is read from the validation years; the test scores are reported next to it.
Both models are scored on identical days: coverage is 1.0 for every model, seed, basin and lead in the validation and test years (asserted in the code).

Seed spread: only 2 random seed(s) per model were affordable on this laptop, so 'min' and 'max' over seeds are a rough guide to the noise, not a confidence interval. cmp_<model> is the day-by-day average of the seeds' forecasts; an average usually scores a little higher than each single seed.

Operations are counted from the formulas in 'formulas' (forward pass, multiply-adds only), not measured. Measured seconds need not scale with that count: it leaves out everything that is not a weight multiplication (softmax, normalisation, moving the day-by-day attention tables through memory) and how well each network uses the processor's threads.
Energy = seconds x 15 W, the nominal design power of the processor: an assumption, no power was measured. No cloud or GPU prices are quoted because none were given.
The learning-rate checks are reported separately (check_seconds) and are not added to seconds_per_model; the tuning of weeks 2-3 is not counted at all.
Warning scores are pooled over the 12 basins; high flow = above the basin's 95th percentile of the training years; onset = only forecasts issued while the river was still at or below that level.

Basins: a median over 12 basins is set by its two middle basins, so a single basin can move it, and the seed spread does not show that. Transformer minus LSTM at 1 / 2 / 3 days ahead, validation years: median NSE -0.089 / -0.050 / -0.028, mean NSE -0.013 / -0.017 / -0.011, LSTM higher in 6 / 10 / 9 of 12 basins; test years: median NSE -0.018 / +0.009 / +0.010, mean NSE +0.004 / -0.003 / -0.002, LSTM higher in 8 / 5 / 5 of 12 basins. The largest median difference on the validation years is at 1 day ahead; there the two models differ most in Murder Creek, GA (NSE 0.620 LSTM, 0.444 Transformer), and without that one basin the median difference is -0.010 instead of -0.089.

Learning-rate check limit: 4 of the 4 candidates (LSTM 0.001, LSTM 0.002, Transformer 0.0003, Transformer 0.001) had their best validation score at the last check of the 300 updates of the check, i.e. they were still improving when it ended. The check therefore ranks the learning rates by how fast they learn at the start, not by where they end after 1000 updates: a lower rate might still have overtaken. The trainer keeps the learning rate constant for both networks (no warm-up, no decay).

Timing: taken under flood.cpu_lock on a 2-core laptop CPU with 4 torch threads, so no other full training job held the CPU, but smoke tests and other light jobs of the project do not wait for that lock and other processes did run alongside: the 1-minute load average at the validation checks of the final trainings was 5.3 to 12.9, where this job alone gives at most about 4, so all times are longer than on an idle laptop. Wall-clock seconds and CPU seconds (summed over threads) are both given; seconds per update is the median time between two consecutive training passes, measured inside the real training. Training time includes the validation checks.

Timing noise: the LSTM seeds took 84 s for 1000 updates and 46 s for 1000 updates; the Transformer seeds 660 s for 1000 updates and 695 s for 1000 updates. Where the same number of updates took a different time, the cause is the state of the laptop (other processes, heat), not the model - so read the time ratios as rough: about 15x per update and 10x per model.
